subject: Pathology
summary: ARDS is a rapid, severe lung injury causing non‑cardiac pulmonary edema and hypoxemia. Diagnosis requires recent insult, bilateral infiltrates, and impaired oxygenation.

sections.p: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome is acute respiratory failure within 7 days of a known insult, with bilateral lung opacities not explained by heart failure or fluid overload.
b: Berlin criteria: timing, imaging, origin of edema, and PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio
PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 300 mmHg on ≥ 5 cm H₂O PEEP defines ARDS

t.b: Does the imaging show bilateral infiltrates? → Confirms the presence of diffuse alveolar damage; helps exclude unilateral disease.
What is the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio? → Determines severity; lower ratios indicate worse oxygenation.
Is cardiac failure contributing? → Normal cardiac pressures support non‑cardiogenic edema; if unavailable, use clinical assessment of volume status.

sections.p: The Berlin definition grades ARDS by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio on PEEP ≥ 5 cm H₂O.
b: Mild: 200 < PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 300 mmHg
Moderate: 100 < PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 200 mmHg
Severe: PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 100 mmHg

sections.p: Identify the precipitating insult; infections dominate in low‑resource settings.
b: Pneumonia (bacterial, viral, TB, malaria‑related lung infection)
Sepsis from intra‑abdominal, urinary, or skin sources
Aspiration of gastric contents
Severe trauma or burns
Pancreatitis
Transfusion‑related acute lung injury

sections.p: Patients develop sudden dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia despite high‑flow oxygen, often with diffuse crackles.
b: Rapid increase in work of breathing
Cyanosis or desaturation < 90 % on room air
Absence of cardiogenic signs (no JVD, clear neck veins)

sections.p: Focused tests confirm the diagnosis, assess severity, and search for the trigger.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis or anemia? → May point to infection or hemorrhage as a trigger.
Is a pathogen identified? → Guides antimicrobial therapy; if unavailable, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics based on local patterns.
Is tissue hypoperfusion present? → High lactate suggests severe sepsis, increasing mortality risk.

sections.p: Early recognition of life‑threatening progression is essential.
b: Refractory hypoxemia despite FiO₂ > 0.8
Rapidly falling PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio
Multi‑organ failure (renal, hepatic, cardiovascular)
Barotrauma from high ventilatory pressures

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide lung‑protective ventilation and supportive care.
b: Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) to limit volutrauma
Plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H₂O
Higher PEEP according to severity tables
Prone positioning for severe ARDS
Conservative fluid strategy after initial resuscitation
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics for suspected infection; de‑escalate when cultures return
Consider neuromuscular blockade if severe asynchrony

sections.p: After stabilization, monitor for recovery and prevent recurrence.
b: Gradual weaning of ventilatory support when oxygenation improves
Pulmonary rehabilitation for residual dyspnea
Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) and infection control to avoid repeat insults
Avoid unnecessary transfusions and aspiration risk

sections.p: Conditions that also cause bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia.
b: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema – distinguished by elevated cardiac pressures, response to diuretics
Pneumonia with consolidation – usually focal, fever, and sputum production
Pulmonary hemorrhage – presents with hemoptysis and drop in hemoglobin

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal early or be falsely abnormal.
b: Normal BNP does not rule out cardiac contribution in mixed shock
Early chest X‑ray may miss subtle infiltrates; CT is more sensitive
PaO₂/FiO₂ can improve transiently with high FiO₂, masking severity

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness with oxygen saturation < 85 % despite supplemental oxygen
New onset confusion or agitation indicating hypoxemic encephalopathy
Rapid drop in blood pressure or urine output suggesting multi‑organ failure

faq.q: Why is ARDS called non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
faq.a: Because the fluid leaks from damaged alveolar capillaries due to inflammation, not from high left‑heart pressures.

faq.q: Can ARDS develop without an infection?
faq.a: Yes; trauma, pancreatitis, aspiration, and transfusion reactions are common non‑infectious triggers.

faq.q: Is high‑flow nasal cannula enough for severe ARDS?
faq.a: Usually not; severe ARDS requires invasive mechanical ventilation with lung‑protective settings.

exam: Explain the Berlin criteria and how they differentiate ARDS from cardiogenic edema.
List the most common causes of ARDS in low‑resource settings and the rationale for early antimicrobial therapy.
Describe the ventilatory strategy for severe ARDS and why low tidal volume is critical.
